title: Sequences, Letters and Position-to-Term Rules
kicker: Cambridge Primary Checkpoint · Mathematics 0096 · Stage 6 · Number
summary: Use letters for numbers that vary, find and use position-to-term rules from repeated addition, and generate terms of square-number sequences.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Understand that a letter can stand for a number that changes (varies) in an addition or subtraction, such as a + b = 15 (6Nc.02)
Use the link between adding the same number again and again and multiplying, to find and use a position-to-term rule (6Nc.03)
Use square numbers to find any term of a sequence when you know its position (6Nc.04)

blocks.text: This page is about patterns and the first ideas of algebra. You will see that a letter can stand for a number, and that a sequence such as 4, 8, 12, 16, … has a rule that lets you jump straight to the 100th term without writing out all the terms before it.
Key words

items: sequence
متتابعة — numbers in order that follow a rule
term
حد — each number in a sequence
position
الترتيب / الموقع — where a term is: 1st, 2nd, 3rd, …
term-to-term rule
قاعدة من حد لحد — how to get from one term to the next (e.g. add 4)
position-to-term rule
قاعدة الموقع — how to get a term from its position (e.g. position × 4)
vary / variable
يتغيّر / متغيّر — a letter that can stand for different numbers
multiple
مضاعف — a number in a times table: 4, 8, 12, … are multiples of 4
square number
عدد مربع — a number multiplied by itself: 5 × 5 = 25

blocks.text: 1. Letters that stand for numbers

In maths we sometimes use a **letter** instead of a number. The letter stands for a **quantity that can vary** (change). Look at a + b = 15. If a is 6, then b must be 9. If a is 10, b must be 5. The letters change, but the rule "they add up to 15" stays the same.

blocks.caption: A bar model: the whole is 15, split into the two parts a and b.

blocks.text: Every pair in the table makes a + b = 15 true. If we are told the numbers must be whole numbers, the decimal pair (7.5, 7.5) is not allowed — always read the conditions in the question.
**Subtraction works in the same way.** m − n = 8 means m is always 8 more than n: if n = 5, m = 13; if n = 12, m = 20.

items: Write the calculation with the number you know put in place of its letter.
Use the inverse operation to find the other letter: if a + b = 15 then b = 15 − a; if m − n = 8 then m = n + 8 and n = m − 8.
Check by putting both numbers back into the original calculation.

blocks.title: A letter is a number, not a word
blocks.text: In a + b = 15, "a" does not mean "apples". It means "a number". Two different letters can stand for the same number (a = 7.5, b = 7.5), but in one calculation the same letter always stands for the same number.
2. Term-to-term and position-to-term rules
Look at the sequence 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, … There are two ways to describe it:

items: **Term-to-term rule:** start at 4 and **add 4** each time. This is good for finding the next term.
**Position-to-term rule:** **term = position × 4**. This lets you find any term straight away.

blocks.caption: Each term is the position multiplied by 4.

blocks.text: **Why does this work?** The 3rd term is 4 + 4 + 4. Adding 4 three times is the same as 3 × 4. In the same way, the 50th term is 4 added 50 times, which is 50 × 4 = **200**. **Repeated addition of the same number is multiplication.**
3. Finding and using a position-to-term rule

items: Make a table with the positions 1, 2, 3, … above the terms.
Find the step (the difference between the terms). If it is the same every time, it is the number you multiply by.
Check with the first term: when the sequence is a times table, term 1 equals the step (e.g. step 7, first term 7).
Write the rule in words: term = position × 7.
Use it: to find the 20th term, do 20 × 7 = 140.
To go backwards (which position is the term 84?), use the inverse: 84 ÷ 7 = 12, so it is the 12th term. If the division does not give a whole number, the number is **not** in the sequence.

blocks.text: 4. Patterns of shapes
Many Checkpoint questions show a pattern made of dots, sticks or tiles. Count how many are added each time — that is the multiplier.

blocks.text: Pattern 15 has 15 columns of 3 dots: 15 × 3 = **45 dots**. Which pattern has 60 dots? 60 ÷ 3 = 20, so **Pattern 20**.
5. Square-number sequences

A **square number** is what you get when you multiply a whole number by itself: 1 × 1 = 1, 2 × 2 = 4, 3 × 3 = 9 and so on. We can write 5 × 5 as 5^{2} ("5 squared"). The name comes from the dot pattern: each square number makes a square.

blocks.text: In the sequence 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, … the rule is: **term = position × position**. So the 10th term is 10 × 10 = **100** and the 12th term is 12 × 12 = **144**.

items: **Spot it:** the differences between square numbers are the odd numbers 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, … — they do not stay the same, so it is not a times-table sequence.
**Is a number in the sequence?** Find a number that multiplies by itself to make it. 81 = 9 × 9, so 81 is the 9th term. 50 is not: 7 × 7 = 49 and 8 × 8 = 64.
**Rules built on squares:** "square the position, then add 1" gives 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, … You still use your square numbers first.

blocks.title: القاعدة اللي لازم تفتكرها
items: قاعدة من حد لحد (term-to-term): بتقولك تزود كام عشان توصل للحد اللي بعده، مثلاً زوّد 4.
قاعدة الموقع (position-to-term): رقم الموقع × الخطوة. الحد رقم 50 في 4، 8، 12 … = 50 × 4 = 200.
لو عايز تعرف العدد ده رقم كام في المتتابعة: اقسم على الخطوة. لو الناتج مش عدد صحيح يبقى العدد مش موجود فيها.
متتابعة المربعات: الحد = الموقع × نفسه (1، 4، 9، 16 …).

blocks.text: Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — a + b = 15. (a) Find b when a = 6. (b) Find a when b = 15. [2 marks]

items: (a) Put 6 in place of a: 6 + b = 15. Inverse: b = 15 − 6 = **9**. Check: 6 + 9 = 15 ✓

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** writing 6 + 15 = 21 for (a). The total is already 15 — b is the missing part.
**Worked example 2** — m − n = 8, where m and n are whole numbers less than 20. (a) Find m when n = 5. (b) Write two more pairs of values for m and n. [2 marks]

items: (b) Choose any n, then add 8 — but m must stay below 20, so n can be at most 11. For example **n = 2, m = 10** and **n = 11, m = 19**.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3** — Here is a sequence: 7, 14, 21, 28, … (a) Write the position-to-term rule. (b) Find the 20th term. [2 marks]

items: The step is +7 every time, and the 1st term is 7, so these are the multiples of 7.
(a) **term = position × 7** (accept "multiply the position by 7").

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** writing "add 7" for (a). That is the term-to-term rule, not the position-to-term rule.

**Worked example 4** — Look at the dot patterns in section 4 (3 dots in Pattern 1, 6 in Pattern 2, 9 in Pattern 3). (a) How many dots are in Pattern 15? (b) Which pattern has exactly 60 dots? [2 marks]

items: Each pattern adds 3 dots, so dots = pattern number × 3.
(b) inverse: 60 ÷ 3 = 20 → **Pattern 20**

blocks.text: **Worked example 5** — The sequence of square numbers starts 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, … (a) What is the 10th term? (b) Is 50 a term in this sequence? Explain. [2 marks]

items: (a) term = position × position = 10 × 10 = **100**
(b) **No.** 7 × 7 = 49 and 8 × 8 = 64. 50 is between them, so no whole-number position gives 50.

blocks.text: **Worked example 6** — Sara is looking at the sequence 6, 12, 18, 24, … She says: "The 50th term is 56, because I add 6 to 50." Is she correct? Explain. [1 mark]

items: Each term is the position **multiplied** by 6 (6 is added again and again, which is multiplication).
**No — she should multiply, not add. The 50th term is 300.** (Check her rule with the 1st term: 1 + 6 = 7, but the 1st term is 6.)

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Mixing up the two rules: "add 5" is term-to-term; "position × 5" is position-to-term.
Adding instead of multiplying to find a far-away term: the 30th term of 3, 6, 9, … is 30 × 3 = 90, not 33.
Thinking 5^{2} means 5 × 2 = 10. It means 5 × 5 = 25.
Saying a number is in the sequence without checking the division is exact: 50 ÷ 4 = 12.5, so 50 is not in 4, 8, 12, …
Counting the first term as position 0. The first term is always position 1.
For a + b = 15, writing b = 15 + a. Use the inverse: b = 15 − a.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: "Complete the table" of positions and terms, often with a far position such as 20 or 100 at the end.
"Draw the next pattern" and "How many tiles/sticks/dots in pattern 10?" — find the multiplier from the pictures.
"Which position is the term 96?" or "Is 75 in the sequence? Explain how you know." — divide, and write a sentence.
Letters: "a + b = 20. Find b when a = 7" or "write two possible pairs"; or tick which pairs make m − n = 6 true.
Square numbers: "Write the 9th term of 1, 4, 9, 16, …" or ring the numbers that are in the sequence.
Technique: always test your rule on the first two terms before using it on the 50th.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Sequences and letters practice
blocks.intro: 14 questions, no calculator. Write down the rule before you calculate. Full working appears when you check.

questions.q: x + y = 20. Find y when x = 13.
p − 9 = q. Find q when p = 25.
questions.e: Put 25 in place of p: 25 − 9 = 16, so q = 16.

questions.q: Which pair of numbers makes a + b = 11 true?
The sequence 5, 10, 15, 20, … continues. Which is its position-to-term rule?
questions.e: 1st term 1 × 5 = 5, 2nd term 2 × 5 = 10 ✓. "Add 5 to the last term" is a term-to-term rule. position + 5 gives 6, 7, 8…; position × 5 + 5 gives 10, 15, 20…

questions.q: The sequence 9, 18, 27, 36, … continues in the same way. What is the 10th term?
questions.e: The step is 9 and the 1st term is 9, so term = position × 9. 10 × 9 = 90.

questions.q: The rule for a sequence is: term = position × 8. Find the 25th term.
The rule for a sequence is: term = position × 4. In which position is the term 96?

questions.p: Yassin makes patterns of squares with sticks. The squares do not touch.

questions.q: (a) How many sticks are in Pattern 12?
questions.e: Pattern 1 has 4 sticks, Pattern 2 has 8, Pattern 3 has 12: each new square adds 4 sticks, so sticks = pattern number × 4. 12 × 4 = 48.

questions.p: Yassin makes patterns of squares with sticks. The squares do not touch.

questions.q: The sequence of square numbers starts 1, 4, 9, 16, … What is the 12th term?
Which number is a term in the sequence 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, …?
The rule for a sequence is: square the position, then add 1. What is the 6th term?
Here is a sequence: 4, 8, 12, 16, … Hassan says: "50 is in this sequence." Is he correct? Explain how you know.
questions.ms: 1 mark: No, with a correct reason, e.g. 50 ÷ 4 = 12.5 (not a whole number) / 50 is not a multiple of 4 / the 12th term is 48 and the 13th term is 52. Do not accept "No" with no reason, or "because 50 is even".
questions.e: Hassan is not correct. term = position × 4, so every term is a multiple of 4. 50 ÷ 4 = 12.5, which is not a whole number. (12 × 4 = 48 and 13 × 4 = 52, so the sequence jumps over 50.)

questions.q: Rana writes the sequence 11, 22, 33, 44, … She keeps going. Which position is the term 154? Choose the correct answer.
questions.e: term = position × 11, so position = 154 ÷ 11 = 14. Check: 14 × 11 = 154 ✓ (143 comes from 154 − 11, which is wrong).

blocks.title: Remember
items: A letter stands for a number that can vary. Use the inverse to find it: a + b = 15 → b = 15 − a.
Term-to-term rule = how to get the next term. Position-to-term rule = how to get any term from its position.
Adding the same number again and again is multiplying: the sequence 7, 14, 21, … has the rule term = position × 7.
To find which position a term is in, divide. Not a whole number → not in the sequence.
Square-number sequence: term = position × position (1, 4, 9, 16, 25, …).
